strengths: Addresses a clearly motivated and underexplored problem: caching acceleration specifically tailored to transformer-based Diffusion Policy, as opposed to prior work focused on image/video diffusion U-Net or DiT backbones.
Solid empirical motivation via similarity matrices/curves (Fig. 1, Fig. 10, Fig. 11) showing non-uniform temporal dynamics and block-specific patterns that justify block-wise adaptive scheduling.

The identification of the 'error surge' phenomenon and its theoretical explanation (Proposition 3.1, linearized error-propagation analysis through LayerNorm/FFN) is a nice piece of technical insight that explains why naive block-wise caching fails and motivates the Bubbling Union Algorithm (BUA).
The proposed Adaptive Caching Scheduler (DP-based optimal schedule search) and BUA are simple, training-free, and computationally cheap (computed once per task offline).

Extensive experimental validation: multiple RoboMimic tasks (PH/MH), Push-T, Block Pushing, Kitchen, a VLA model (RDT-1B on ManiSkill), and a real-world Franka arm deployment, plus thorough ablations (choice of similarity metric, hyperparameter n, combination with DDIM) in the appendix.
Good supporting visualizations (cache error heatmaps, feature heatmaps, inter-episode similarity) that substantiate claims about episode homogeneity and cache reliability.
Reports both FLOPs/speedup and practical metrics (inference frequency, end-to-end latency) in real-world tests, showing tangible benefits for real-time control.
weaknesses: Baseline comparison is relatively narrow: only 'Uniform' and an adapted 'TeaCache' are compared; several transformer-diffusion caching methods cited in related work (FORA, δ-DiT, Learning-to-Cache, token-wise caching) are not empirically compared even in adapted form, making it harder to assess relative advantage.

The 'lossless' framing is optimistic given that Table 1/Table 3 show clear performance collapses under certain hyperparameter settings (e.g., BAC(S=5, n=3) average success 0.07, MH Square at S=7 dropping from 0.76 to 0.39), indicating the method is sensitive to the joint choice of S and n and not uniformly robust across tasks.

The method requires per-task offline computation and tuning of at least two hyperparameters (S, n), and their interaction is shown to be non-trivial (Table 3); this adds practical overhead to what is billed as a plug-and-play, training-free method.

Real-world validation is limited to a single manipulation task (bag pick-and-release) on one hardware setup with qualitative rollouts only; no repeated-trial statistics or multiple task variety are reported to support generalizability claims in real deployments.

The limitations section is a single sentence and does not discuss computational/memory overhead of the DP solver at scale, sensitivity to hyperparameters, or applicability to backbones beyond DiT-style Diffusion Policy/VLA.

Reliance on the 'high episode homogeneity' assumption (computed once per task) may not hold in more diverse, open-world, or long-horizon tasks; the evidence provided (Appendix A.15) is restricted to the same benchmarks used for evaluation, so generalization to less homogeneous settings is untested.

Some experimental design choices (e.g., choosing Cosine as default metric, n=5 default) appear to be selected post hoc from the ablation grid rather than justified a priori, raising minor concerns about implicit tuning on the test set of tasks.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: diffusion-policy inference latency is a real bottleneck for real-time robot control, and the paper is one of the first to systematically study caching acceleration specifically for transformer-based Diffusion Policy rather than image/video diffusion.

The key empirical observations (non-uniform temporal similarity, block-specific similarity patterns, and the 'error surge' phenomenon caused by inter-block error propagation through FFNs) are interesting and are supported by a reasonably careful set of diagnostic experiments (Fig. 1, 4, 14, 15).

The proposed Adaptive Caching Scheduler is grounded in a clean, exact dynamic-programming formulation for maximizing global cached-feature similarity, which is a principled and efficient (non-exhaustive) way to select cache-update timesteps.

The Bubbling Union Algorithm is a simple, well-motivated fix for the discovered failure mode, and a first-order theoretical analysis (Proposition 3.1) of how FFN blocks amplify upstream caching error is provided to justify the design.

Extensive empirical evaluation across a wide range of settings: real-robot deployment (Franka arm), multiple RoboMimic tasks with both PH/MH data, Push-T, Block Pushing, Kitchen, and a VLA model (RDT-1B on ManiSkill) — this breadth is uncommon and strengthens external validity.

Thorough ablations (Unified ACS vs Block-wise ACS vs Block-wise ACS+BUA), sensitivity analysis on hyperparameter n, comparison of similarity metrics (MSE/L1/Wasserstein/Cosine), and an additional experiment combining BAC with DDIM — these support the claimed design choices reasonably well.

Reasonable reproducibility effort: hyperparameters, datasets, and proofs are documented in the appendix, and a large appendix provides extensive supporting visualizations (feature heatmaps, episode-homogeneity evidence).
weaknesses: Baseline comparison is fairly narrow: only a self-constructed 'Uniform' baseline and an adapted 'TeaCache' (originally designed for video diffusion) are compared quantitatively; several directly relevant caching methods discussed in Related Work (DeepCache, ForA, Learning-to-cache, δ-DiT, token-wise caching) are cited but never empirically compared, making it hard to assess how much of the improvement is attributable to the specific block-wise/DP/BUA design versus simply having a stronger baseline.

The 'lossless'/'~3x for free' framing in the abstract and conclusion is not fully consistent with the results: Table 3 shows clear performance collapse for aggressive caching on hard tasks (e.g., Tool_hang success 0.00 at S=5, Transport_mh 0.26/0.50 at S=5), and success on some tasks only recovers near full precision at large S (e.g., S=20), which is a much smaller speedup than headline numbers suggest.

Occasional cases where BAC reportedly slightly exceeds full-precision performance (e.g., Table 1 AVG 0.79 vs 0.76) are not explained; without variance/error bars across the 3 seeds, it is unclear whether these differences (and other close comparisons) are statistically meaningful or within noise.

The method requires task-specific offline computation of the caching schedule (via ACS+BUA) and per-task/per-domain tuning of hyperparameters n and S (different values used for simulation vs. real-world, and further tuned per task in Table 3), which is somewhat in tension with the 'plug-and-play, training-free' framing, since deployment to a new task requires nontrivial recalibration.

The theoretical analysis (Proposition 3.1) is a first-order linear approximation under several simplifying assumptions (bounded weights/second derivatives, LayerNorm variance lower bound) and is only validated indirectly via a correlation coefficient in a toy experiment; it does not provide a quantitative error bound that is used operationally by the algorithm (BUA instead relies on a heuristic ℓ1-based error proxy).

Reproducibility is currently incomplete: code is promised to be released but not yet available at review time, and some appendix figures (e.g., Fig. 14–25 feature heatmaps) are very small/hard to read, limiting their evidentiary value as presented.

Presentation issues: inconsistent capitalization/naming (e.g., 'Robomimic' vs 'RoboMimic'), some placeholder-looking bibliography entries ('Placeholder Publisher', 'Submitted to Some Conference'), and dense/cramped figures reduce overall polish and clarity.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated, practically important problem: accelerating transformer-based Diffusion Policy for real-time robot control, which is underexplored compared to image/video diffusion caching.

Clear empirical motivation via similarity-matrix visualizations showing non-uniform temporal redundancy and block-specific patterns, which justifies the need for block-wise (rather than uniform) caching schedules.

The Adaptive Caching Scheduler is grounded in a clean dynamic-programming formulation that efficiently finds a provably optimal (within the discretized similarity-maximization objective) update schedule instead of relying on heuristics or brute-force search.

The paper identifies and rigorously analyzes a non-obvious failure mode (the 'error surge' phenomenon in FFN blocks under naive block-wise scheduling), backed by a first-order theoretical analysis (Proposition 3.1, proved in the appendix) and toy experiments showing strong correlation (r≈0.99) between upstream and downstream errors.

The Bubbling Union Algorithm is a simple, low-overhead, training-free fix motivated directly by this analysis, and ablations (Fig. 7b) convincingly show it is necessary to recover full-precision performance once block-wise scheduling is introduced.

Extensive experimental validation: multiple RoboMimic tasks (PH/MH), Push-T, Kitchen, Block Pushing, a VLA model (RDT-1B on ManiSkill), and a real-world robot arm deployment, along with strong ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (n, similarity metric choice), and compatibility with DDIM samplers.
Good-faith reproducibility efforts: detailed hyperparameters, full derivations in the appendix, extensive supplementary visualizations, and an explicit reproducibility/ethics statement.

Demonstrated near-lossless (even occasionally improved) success rates with 3-3.6x speedups across most benchmarks, and clear behavioral/qualitative differences vs. baselines in the real-world deployment (reduced latency-induced desynchronization).
weaknesses: Real-world evaluation is limited to a single manipulation task (soft bag pick-and-place) on one robot arm, with only qualitative trajectory comparisons in Fig. 6; no reported number of trials, variance, or statistical significance for the real-world success rates/frequencies.

Baseline comparisons are relatively narrow: only 'Uniform' and an adapted 'TeaCache' (originally designed for video diffusion) are compared against, despite the related-work section citing several transformer/DiT-specific caching methods (e.g., FORA, ToCa/token-wise caching, δ-DiT, DiTFastAttn) that could plausibly be adapted as stronger baselines; the paper does not justify why these were excluded.

The method's core efficiency claim relies on an offline, per-task precomputed caching schedule derived from ground-truth features on sampled demo episodes, which depends on the empirically observed 'episode homogeneity' assumption; robustness to out-of-distribution episodes/observations at test time is not analyzed beyond a brief limitation statement about low base-model accuracy.

BUA's Remark 3.1 explicitly ignores update-induced upstream errors for tractability, and the top-n hyperparameter for BUA requires per-task/per-S tuning (shown in Appendix A.7) without an automatic selection procedure, adding practical deployment complexity.

Some tasks show fragile behavior at aggressive caching budgets (e.g., BAC(S=5) achieving 0.00 success on Tool_hang_ph in Table 3), indicating the method's 'lossless' claims are budget-dependent and can still collapse under tight compute budgets, which somewhat undercuts the generality of the headline 3x speedup claim.

FLOPs are used as the main efficiency metric for most simulation experiments rather than measured wall-clock latency, which may not directly translate to real hardware speedups (only the single real-world task reports actual latency/frequency).

Presentation is dense in places (heavy reliance on multi-panel figures without fully self-contained captions, e.g., Fig. 4 and the large appendix heatmap grids), which could hinder readability for reviewers/readers not deeply familiar with the specific caching literature.
